summary: Extends RSVP-TE so that Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) entities can be set up and configured together with the signaling of a label-switched path. This keeps OAM and connection setup in sync and avoids false alarms.

plainLanguage.summary: When you build a road, you should turn on the traffic cameras at the same time. This lets the network set up its health checks when it sets up the path.

what are mep and mip in mpls
subtitle: Setting up OAM health checks inside the same RSVP-TE signaling that builds the label switched path.

tldr.problem: OAM monitoring must be switched on and off in step with the connection it watches, or it raises false alarms, and separate manual configuration is slow and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: RSVP-TE gains two LSP attribute flags, an OAM Configuration TLV, two Admin_Status bits and a new error code, so OAM is configured during Path and Resv signaling with alarms held off until both ends are ready.
tldr.outcome: OAM entities and functions can be created, adjusted and deleted together with an end-to-end LSP. The RFC defines no OAM types itself, so technology-specific documents must fill them in.

today: RFC 7260 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC defines no OAM Types itself and leaves technology-specific sub-TLVs to separate documents.

sections.title: Why Configure OAM with Signaling
sections.content:
Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) functions monitor the health and performance of connections. They must be activated and deactivated in sync with connection commissioning and decommissioning to avoid spurious alarms. Some technologies set up OAM entities automatically with the connection, while others need extra configuration.

Binding OAM setup to GMPLS signaling avoids a separate configuration step after the connection is up, which adds delay and invites misconfiguration. The scope is end-to-end OAM for an LSP signaled with RSVP-TE. Segments and tandem connections are out of scope. The mechanism is an additional option for bootstrapping OAM and does not replace others such as LSP ping (RFC 4379).
sections.plainLanguage: If you set up the alarm and the road at different times, the alarm shouts that something is missing. Doing both together stops the false alarms.

sections.title: Requirements Behind the Design
sections.content:
The RFC collects requirements from MPLS OAM (RFC 4377), MPLS-TP (RFC 5654 and RFC 5860) and Ethernet connectivity fault management on PBB-TE connections. The control plane must be able to configure OAM maintenance points when a path is set up or changed.

For wavelength, TDM and packet data planes, the operator MUST be able to request OAM setup for a signaled LSP, enable or disable alarms, set the frequency of continuity check messages per LSP, and set common parameters for proactive performance monitoring. A minimal set of OAM features MUST also be allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: Different kinds of networks need different checks, so the design has to be flexible enough to switch things on, quiet the alarms, and choose how often to check.

sections.title: Setting Up, Changing and Removing OAM
sections.content:
There are two kinds of maintenance points. MEPs sit at the ends of an LSP and start and end OAM messages, while MIPs sit at transit nodes and react to some OAM messages.

Setup. The initiator first configures OAM locally, but its OAM source MUST NOT send messages until the LSP is up. It sends the Path message with the "OAM Alarms Enabled" Admin_Status flag cleared. The remote end configures OAM from the Path message, or SHOULD send a PathErr if it cannot. It replies with a Resv message carrying the flags and the OAM Configuration TLV. A second Path/Resv exchange with the alarms flag set turns alarms on at both ends.

Adjustment. The LSP is re-signaled with alarms cleared and the new TLV, parameters are changed on the sink and the source, and a later exchange re-enables alarms. The receiver SHOULD NOT weaken the requested parameters, such as lowering the monitoring frequency.

Deletion. Alarms are disabled first, then the LSP is re-signaled with the MEP and MIP flags cleared and no OAM Configuration TLV. Source functions are removed before sinks so OAM messages do not leak outside the LSP.

If an egress node does not support these extensions it silently ignores them, so the ingress detects the missing information in the Resv message and SHOULD tear down the LSP and signal it again without OAM.
sections.plainLanguage: First both ends get their gear ready while the alarm is muted. Then the alarm is switched on. To stop, you mute the alarm first, then remove the gear.

sections.title: The RSVP-TE Extensions
sections.content:
Two bits are added to the Attribute Flags TLV from RFC 5420: bit 10, "OAM MEP entities desired", and bit 11, "OAM MIP entities desired". The MIP bit MUST NOT be set unless the MEP bit is set. Two Admin_Status bits are also added: bit 23, "OAM Flows Enabled" (M), and bit 24, "OAM Alarms Enabled" (O).

The OAM Configuration TLV has type 3. It carries an OAM Type, a Reserved field and sub-TLVs, and may appear in the LSP_ATTRIBUTES or LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES object. It MUST be zero-padded to 4-octet alignment. This document defines no OAM Types. The one generic sub-TLV is the OAM Function Flags sub-TLV (type 1), which MUST come first. Its bits select Continuity Check (0), Connectivity Verification (1), Fault Management Signal (2), PM/Loss (3), PM/Delay (4) and PM/Throughput (5). At most one technology-specific sub-TLV is allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages get a few new check boxes: do you want health checks at the ends, in the middle, and which kinds. There is also a small form for extra details.

sections.title: Errors and Point-to-Multipoint LSPs
sections.content:
A new RSVP error code, 40 "OAM Problem", carries six values in a PathErr message: 1 MEP establishment not supported, 2 MIP establishment not supported, 3 Unsupported OAM Type, 4 Configuration Error, 5 OAM Type Mismatch and 6 Unsupported OAM Function. The Configuration Error value is used when the hierarchy is broken, for example when an OAM Configuration TLV is present without the MEP flag.

For point-to-multipoint LSPs, the root MUST keep the OAM configuration identical in every Path message, and branch nodes MUST copy it unchanged. There is no per-leaf negotiation. A leaf that cannot accept the parameters reports it through the RRO Attributes sub-object by clearing the MEP bit in its Resv message. If some leaves fail, one suggested fix is two P2MP LSPs, one with OAM and one without. The exact procedures are left to technology-specific documents.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stop along the way cannot do what was asked, it sends back a note saying which part it cannot do. With one sender and many receivers, everyone must follow the same plan.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Automatic OAM setup adds a new angle to the security issues in RFC 3473. A remote attacker could overload a network element by requesting frequent periodic liveliness monitoring of many LSPs. Message integrity and node authentication prevent this, and the RSVP security procedures in RFC 2747 can be used. RFC 5920 gives a broader discussion of MPLS and GMPLS security.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad actor could ask a device to run so many checks that it gets tired. Making sure messages are real and from trusted neighbors prevents that.
